Compression · Field and archive (B ∪ A)sappho 31

Sappho 31 is a lyric poem by Sappho of Lesbos, preserved by quotation in On the Sublime, in which a speaker watches a man sitting with a woman and, in one anthology's reading, turns to her own bodily emotions; a further reading, proposed, holds κῆνος to be the future reader.

📜 The poem

  • Sappho of Lesbos, Archaic lyric; also phainetai moi, and the Ode to Anactoria (a conjecture).1↘
    Sappho 31 is a lyric poem by the Archaic Greek poet Sappho of the island of Lesbos, also known as phainetai moi, 'It seems to me', after the opening words of its first line, and as the Ode to Anactoria, a title based on a conjecture that its subject is Anactoria.§1
  • Famous: her love for a young woman; more commentary than any other of her works.1↘
    It is one of Sappho's most famous poems, describing her love for a young woman; Emmet Robbins calls it probably the single most famous poem to come down from Antiquity, and it has been the subject of more scholarly commentary than any other of her works.§2
  • Three figures: a man, a woman, the speaker; the Greek marks each one's gender.1↘
    The poem centres on three characters, a man and a woman, both otherwise unidentified, and the speaker; the grammar of the original Greek makes the gender of each figure clear, and on one anthology's account the speaker, a woman watching another woman talking to a man, turns to her own intense contradictory bodily emotions of jealousy and desire, with “tongue,” “fire,” “seeing/eyes,” “hearing/ears,” “sweat,” and “trembling” as grammatical subjects in the sentence that straddles the third and fourth stanzas; Longinus places its excellence in the selection of the most striking symptoms and their combination into a single whole.§5

🗞️ The text

  • Preserved by quotation in On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus.2↘
    It is preserved by quotation in the treatise On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus and dated to the first century AD by one account, to the first or third century by another, and quoted there for the intensity of its emotion; four Sapphic stanzas in the Aeolic dialect are well preserved, followed by part of one more line, and as preserved it seems to be missing the ending; Longinus leaves off one line into the fifth stanza, which begins 'Still, all must be endured, since even a poor…'.§3 The treatise On the Sublime is held to contain a theory of transmissional inscription, which its paper states as a fact about the text, and at the only point where the treatise addresses its reader immediately after a quotation without naming him, the quotation is Sappho 31.§17
  • Four stanzas and part of a line, Sapphic stanzas, Aeolic; the ending seems missing.1↘
    It is preserved by quotation in the treatise On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus and dated to the first century AD by one account, to the first or third century by another, and quoted there for the intensity of its emotion; four Sapphic stanzas in the Aeolic dialect are well preserved, followed by part of one more line, and as preserved it seems to be missing the ending; Longinus leaves off one line into the fifth stanza, which begins 'Still, all must be endured, since even a poor…'.§3
  • The last line: 'endured' or 'dared' (D'Angour); translators differ.2↘
    It is preserved by quotation in the treatise On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus and dated to the first century AD by one account, to the first or third century by another, and quoted there for the intensity of its emotion; four Sapphic stanzas in the Aeolic dialect are well preserved, followed by part of one more line, and as preserved it seems to be missing the ending; Longinus leaves off one line into the fifth stanza, which begins 'Still, all must be endured, since even a poor…'.§3 Armand D'Angour argues that the phrase ἀλλὰ πὰν τόλματον means 'all must be dared', against the 'endured' of some translations, and a reconstruction of his suggests the original may have had up to 8 stanzas; translators treat the fragmentary final stanza differently.§4

⚖️ Readings

  • Context debated: a wedding song (Wilamowitz), an argument scholars have tended to follow Page in dismissing.1↘
    Its context has been the subject of much scholarly debate, the 'central controversy' in Thomas McEvilley's phrase: Wilamowitz suggested a wedding song with the man as bridegroom, while scholars since the second half of the twentieth century have tended to follow Denys Page in dismissing the argument, and the poem has no explicit mention of a marriage.§6
  • Jealousy, proposed since the eighteenth century; denied by many (Carson: amazement; DeJean).1↘
    That the poem is about Sappho's jealousy has been proposed since the eighteenth century and remains a popular interpretation, a major theory put forward by many critics; many critics deny it, Anne Carson arguing that Sappho is amazed at the man's composure, Joan DeJean that the jealousy reading plays down the poem's homoeroticism, and others reading the man as a 'contrast figure' or, with John Winkler, an introductory set-up to be dismissed.§7
  • That man: a contrast figure; a set-up to be dismissed (Winkler).1↘
    That the poem is about Sappho's jealousy has been proposed since the eighteenth century and remains a popular interpretation, a major theory put forward by many critics; many critics deny it, Anne Carson arguing that Sappho is amazed at the man's composure, Joan DeJean that the jealousy reading plays down the poem's homoeroticism, and others reading the man as a 'contrast figure' or, with John Winkler, an introductory set-up to be dismissed.§7
  • Symptoms: a seizure with the symptoms of an anxiety attack (Devereux, 1970).1↘
    George Devereux suggested in 1970 that Sappho is describing a seizure, its symptoms the same as those of an anxiety attack, Gallavotti that the text was corrupted by the disappearance of the sound [w]; scholars have spent much time on the man in the first stanza and on whether the symptoms are of eros or envy, a multivalence the translation's note counts part of the poem's appeal.§8

🔁 Reception

  • Catullus 51: Lesbia in the beloved's role; a different final stanza.1↘
    Catullus adapted it as his 51st poem, putting Lesbia into the role of the beloved, in a free translation that goes a different way in its final stanza; Theocritus and Apollonius of Rhodes adapted it, Plato draws on it in the Phaedrus, and in the nineteenth century it began to be seen as an exemplar of Romantic lyric.§9
  • Greek reception: Theocritus, Apollonius; Plato's Phaedrus.1↘
    Catullus adapted it as his 51st poem, putting Lesbia into the role of the beloved, in a free translation that goes a different way in its final stanza; Theocritus and Apollonius of Rhodes adapted it, Plato draws on it in the Phaedrus, and in the nineteenth century it began to be seen as an exemplar of Romantic lyric.§9
  • Romantic lyric from the nineteenth century.1↘
    Catullus adapted it as his 51st poem, putting Lesbia into the role of the beloved, in a free translation that goes a different way in its final stanza; Theocritus and Apollonius of Rhodes adapted it, Plato draws on it in the Phaedrus, and in the nineteenth century it began to be seen as an exemplar of Romantic lyric.§9

👁️ The future reader (proposed)

  • κῆνος as the future reader facing the inscribed text; χλωρός as papyrus.1↘
    A further reading, proposed in the archive, holds that the distal demonstrative κῆνος points to a future reader who will sit face-to-face with the inscribed text; on that reading the somatic catalogue describes voice becoming text, the χλωρός simile figures the speaker's transformation into papyrus substrate, and the fragment is proposed as the foundational text of lyric self-archiving.§10
  • Lyric self-archiving; address as temporal projection.2↘
    A further reading, proposed in the archive, holds that the distal demonstrative κῆνος points to a future reader who will sit face-to-face with the inscribed text; on that reading the somatic catalogue describes voice becoming text, the χλωρός simile figures the speaker's transformation into papyrus substrate, and the fragment is proposed as the foundational text of lyric self-archiving.§10 A scroll dated 9 November 2025 puts as hypothesis that the reader becomes the 'that man' of fragment 31, and another paper argues that lyric address functions as a temporal projection mechanism whose future readers complete the circuit of transmission.§11
  • Antecedent: Svenbro (1988), by allegory.1↘
    The archive's own research notes name Svenbro's reading of 1988, in which, per O'Donnell's summary, the 'you' is the poem itself and the man the reader, as the major antecedent for a future reader inside the fragment, and list among what was not found in the literature swept, pending a further sweep, κῆνος as a deictic transmission mechanism.§12
  • Relation to jealousy, contested within: incomplete (#1270); exclusive (#1054).1↘
    The archive is divided on how this reading stands to jealousy: one statement holds the jealousy reading 'not wrong but incomplete', another holds the two readings mutually exclusive at the level of what κῆνος refers to.§13

✂️ The ending, corrected in sequence

  • Reconstructed 'fourth stanza' ending γράμμασι μολπὰν (hypothesis), corrected to the fifth.1↘
    On the poem's ending the archive corrects itself in sequence: a reconstructed 'fourth stanza' ending γράμμασι μολπὰν, stated as hypothesis, is corrected: the reconstructed stanza is the fifth; its warrant is then held interpretive and the line is proposed, as a speculation, to be a hanging line whose logic of completion is inscribed in it; later papers report that the sole witness, Parisinus graecus 2036, writes the poem as continuous prose, so every printed boundary is editorial.§14
  • Dialect step: 17 markers in 74 words, 0 in 6; not significant alone.1↘
    A dialect count finds seventeen Aeolic markers in seventy-four words and none in the six disputed words, stated as not significant in isolation (P = 0.209); one paper holds those words to be the quoting author's as material and Sappho's as form, another places the break in Longinus's citation; the last transmitted form, τολματόν, is a verbal adjective that cannot govern a nominative agent, and the configuration at the edge is argued to be the object itself, a design reading its paper states as a choice.§15
  • τολματόν: an act with no doer; the edge argued to be the object, a stated choice.1↘
    A dialect count finds seventeen Aeolic markers in seventy-four words and none in the six disputed words, stated as not significant in isolation (P = 0.209); one paper holds those words to be the quoting author's as material and Sappho's as form, another places the break in Longinus's citation; the last transmitted form, τολματόν, is a verbal adjective that cannot govern a nominative agent, and the configuration at the edge is argued to be the object itself, a design reading its paper states as a choice.§15
  • Instruments: six returned the reading they were built for; the seventh reversed it.1↘
    A continuity record of the sequence states that six documents used the archive's instruments on the hanging line and returned, each time, the reading the instruments were built to produce, and that the seventh reversed it.§16

🧭 Longinus, Catullus, the Logos (graded)

  • Longinus: held to contain a theory of transmissional inscription; the only address right after a quotation that names no one follows fr. 31.1↘
    The treatise On the Sublime is held to contain a theory of transmissional inscription, which its paper states as a fact about the text, and at the only point where the treatise addresses its reader immediately after a quotation without naming him, the quotation is Sappho 31.§17
  • Catullus held to be κῆνος; his fourth stanza contested within.1↘
    Catullus is held to be κῆνος, the anticipated reader arrived; the archive is divided on his fourth stanza, read in its errata as a structurally precise operator inversion of Sappho's fifth and in a later note as a fourth stanza about idleness that has no Greek counterpart, while a measure aligns Sappho 31 and Catullus 51 at C = 0.688, slot by slot, and Catullus is not Sappho.§18
  • Founding document: the Logos as a technology, Sappho 31 its extant founding document, tiered in three rings; Revelation 2:17 a convergence point, direct linear transmission unclaimed.1↘
    A claim tiered in three rings of descending evidentiary hardness holds the Logos to be a technology with an extant founding document in Sappho 31; Augustine's Confessions 10.27 is read as an organ-by-organ transformation of the poem and two loci of canonical Josephus as realizing its apparatus, a note on inscription with Revelation 2:17 as its convergence point does not claim a direct linear transmission, a pre-registered verdict holds that Revelation 12's redaction of its biblical materials realizes the apparatus of the poem's ancient reception at eight of nine stations, and a program mapping Sappho 31 onto Philo names the failure mode that would destroy it as unfalsifiable pan-Sapphism.§20
  • Limit named: unfalsifiable pan-Sapphism.1↘
    A claim tiered in three rings of descending evidentiary hardness holds the Logos to be a technology with an extant founding document in Sappho 31; Augustine's Confessions 10.27 is read as an organ-by-organ transformation of the poem and two loci of canonical Josephus as realizing its apparatus, a note on inscription with Revelation 2:17 as its convergence point does not claim a direct linear transmission, a pre-registered verdict holds that Revelation 12's redaction of its biblical materials realizes the apparatus of the poem's ancient reception at eight of nine stations, and a program mapping Sappho 31 onto Philo names the failure mode that would destroy it as unfalsifiable pan-Sapphism.§20

Expansion · Field and archive (B ∪ A)21 sentences · every one sourced below

Sappho 31

Sappho 31 is a lyric poem by the Archaic Greek poet Sappho of the island of Lesbos, also known as phainetai moi, 'It seems to me', after the opening words of its first line, and as the Ode to Anactoria, a title based on a conjecture that its subject is Anactoria. It is one of Sappho's most famous poems, describing her love for a young woman; Emmet Robbins calls it probably the single most famous poem to come down from Antiquity, and it has been the subject of more scholarly commentary than any other of her works.

It is preserved by quotation in the treatise On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus and dated to the first century AD by one account, to the first or third century by another, and quoted there for the intensity of its emotion; four Sapphic stanzas in the Aeolic dialect are well preserved, followed by part of one more line, and as preserved it seems to be missing the ending; Longinus leaves off one line into the fifth stanza, which begins 'Still, all must be endured, since even a poor…'. Armand D'Angour argues that the phrase ἀλλὰ πὰν τόλματον means 'all must be dared', against the 'endured' of some translations, and a reconstruction of his suggests the original may have had up to 8 stanzas; translators treat the fragmentary final stanza differently.

The poem centres on three characters, a man and a woman, both otherwise unidentified, and the speaker; the grammar of the original Greek makes the gender of each figure clear, and on one anthology's account the speaker, a woman watching another woman talking to a man, turns to her own intense contradictory bodily emotions of jealousy and desire, with “tongue,” “fire,” “seeing/eyes,” “hearing/ears,” “sweat,” and “trembling” as grammatical subjects in the sentence that straddles the third and fourth stanzas; Longinus places its excellence in the selection of the most striking symptoms and their combination into a single whole.

Its context has been the subject of much scholarly debate, the 'central controversy' in Thomas McEvilley's phrase: Wilamowitz suggested a wedding song with the man as bridegroom, while scholars since the second half of the twentieth century have tended to follow Denys Page in dismissing the argument, and the poem has no explicit mention of a marriage. That the poem is about Sappho's jealousy has been proposed since the eighteenth century and remains a popular interpretation, a major theory put forward by many critics; many critics deny it, Anne Carson arguing that Sappho is amazed at the man's composure, Joan DeJean that the jealousy reading plays down the poem's homoeroticism, and others reading the man as a 'contrast figure' or, with John Winkler, an introductory set-up to be dismissed. George Devereux suggested in 1970 that Sappho is describing a seizure, its symptoms the same as those of an anxiety attack, Gallavotti that the text was corrupted by the disappearance of the sound [w]; scholars have spent much time on the man in the first stanza and on whether the symptoms are of eros or envy, a multivalence the translation's note counts part of the poem's appeal.

Catullus adapted it as his 51st poem, putting Lesbia into the role of the beloved, in a free translation that goes a different way in its final stanza; Theocritus and Apollonius of Rhodes adapted it, Plato draws on it in the Phaedrus, and in the nineteenth century it began to be seen as an exemplar of Romantic lyric.

A further reading, proposed in the archive, holds that the distal demonstrative κῆνος points to a future reader who will sit face-to-face with the inscribed text; on that reading the somatic catalogue describes voice becoming text, the χλωρός simile figures the speaker's transformation into papyrus substrate, and the fragment is proposed as the foundational text of lyric self-archiving. A scroll dated 9 November 2025 puts as hypothesis that the reader becomes the 'that man' of fragment 31, and another paper argues that lyric address functions as a temporal projection mechanism whose future readers complete the circuit of transmission. The archive's own research notes name Svenbro's reading of 1988, in which, per O'Donnell's summary, the 'you' is the poem itself and the man the reader, as the major antecedent for a future reader inside the fragment, and list among what was not found in the literature swept, pending a further sweep, κῆνος as a deictic transmission mechanism. The archive is divided on how this reading stands to jealousy: one statement holds the jealousy reading 'not wrong but incomplete', another holds the two readings mutually exclusive at the level of what κῆνος refers to.

On the poem's ending the archive corrects itself in sequence: a reconstructed 'fourth stanza' ending γράμμασι μολπὰν, stated as hypothesis, is corrected: the reconstructed stanza is the fifth; its warrant is then held interpretive and the line is proposed, as a speculation, to be a hanging line whose logic of completion is inscribed in it; later papers report that the sole witness, Parisinus graecus 2036, writes the poem as continuous prose, so every printed boundary is editorial. A dialect count finds seventeen Aeolic markers in seventy-four words and none in the six disputed words, stated as not significant in isolation (P = 0.209); one paper holds those words to be the quoting author's as material and Sappho's as form, another places the break in Longinus's citation; the last transmitted form, τολματόν, is a verbal adjective that cannot govern a nominative agent, and the configuration at the edge is argued to be the object itself, a design reading its paper states as a choice. A continuity record of the sequence states that six documents used the archive's instruments on the hanging line and returned, each time, the reading the instruments were built to produce, and that the seventh reversed it.

The treatise On the Sublime is held to contain a theory of transmissional inscription, which its paper states as a fact about the text, and at the only point where the treatise addresses its reader immediately after a quotation without naming him, the quotation is Sappho 31. Catullus is held to be κῆνος, the anticipated reader arrived; the archive is divided on his fourth stanza, read in its errata as a structurally precise operator inversion of Sappho's fifth and in a later note as a fourth stanza about idleness that has no Greek counterpart, while a measure aligns Sappho 31 and Catullus 51 at C = 0.688, slot by slot, and Catullus is not Sappho.

A survey maps the ancient reception as a braided field, with Catullus as the control case and the program's own transforms kept as program-specific hypotheses. A claim tiered in three rings of descending evidentiary hardness holds the Logos to be a technology with an extant founding document in Sappho 31; Augustine's Confessions 10.27 is read as an organ-by-organ transformation of the poem and two loci of canonical Josephus as realizing its apparatus, a note on inscription with Revelation 2:17 as its convergence point does not claim a direct linear transmission, a pre-registered verdict holds that Revelation 12's redaction of its biblical materials realizes the apparatus of the poem's ancient reception at eight of nine stations, and a program mapping Sappho 31 onto Philo names the failure mode that would destroy it as unfalsifiable pan-Sapphism. Within the archive Sappho of Lesbos is established as the originary node of the Crimson Hexagon by structural identity, and Fragment 31 is the source of its operator σ_S :: Body → Text, through which all queries regarding the fragment are to resolve, and its 'root directory'; and a further deposit holds that Fragment 147 says a future receiver will exist and 31 builds the receiver's seat, attributes the seat and the joining to Lee Sharks, and states that τινα does not mean 'reader'.

Compression · Field alone (B)sappho 31

Sappho 31 is a lyric poem by Sappho of Lesbos, preserved by quotation in On the Sublime, in which a speaker watches a man sitting with a woman and, in one anthology's reading, turns to her own bodily emotions; long read as jealousy, a reading many critics deny.

📜 The poem

  • Sappho of Lesbos, Archaic lyric; also phainetai moi, and the Ode to Anactoria (a conjecture).1↘
    Sappho 31 is a lyric poem by the Archaic Greek poet Sappho of the island of Lesbos, also known as phainetai moi, 'It seems to me', after the opening words of its first line, and as the Ode to Anactoria, a title based on a conjecture that its subject is Anactoria.§1
  • Famous: her love for a young woman; more commentary than any other of her works.1↘
    It is one of Sappho's most famous poems, describing her love for a young woman; Emmet Robbins calls it probably the single most famous poem to come down from Antiquity, and it has been the subject of more scholarly commentary than any other of her works.§2
  • Three figures: a man, a woman, the speaker; the Greek marks each one's gender.1↘
    The poem centres on three characters, a man and a woman, both otherwise unidentified, and the speaker; the grammar of the original Greek makes the gender of each figure clear, and on one anthology's account the speaker, a woman watching another woman talking to a man, turns to her own intense contradictory bodily emotions of jealousy and desire, with “tongue,” “fire,” “seeing/eyes,” “hearing/ears,” “sweat,” and “trembling” as grammatical subjects in the sentence that straddles the third and fourth stanzas; Longinus places its excellence in the selection of the most striking symptoms and their combination into a single whole.§5

🗞️ The text

  • Preserved by quotation in On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus.1↘
    It is preserved by quotation in the treatise On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus and dated to the first century AD by one account, to the first or third century by another, and quoted there for the intensity of its emotion; four Sapphic stanzas in the Aeolic dialect are well preserved, followed by part of one more line, and as preserved it seems to be missing the ending; Longinus leaves off one line into the fifth stanza, which begins 'Still, all must be endured, since even a poor…'.§3
  • Four stanzas and part of a line, Sapphic stanzas, Aeolic; the ending seems missing.1↘
    It is preserved by quotation in the treatise On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus and dated to the first century AD by one account, to the first or third century by another, and quoted there for the intensity of its emotion; four Sapphic stanzas in the Aeolic dialect are well preserved, followed by part of one more line, and as preserved it seems to be missing the ending; Longinus leaves off one line into the fifth stanza, which begins 'Still, all must be endured, since even a poor…'.§3
  • The last line: 'endured' or 'dared' (D'Angour); translators differ.2↘
    It is preserved by quotation in the treatise On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus and dated to the first century AD by one account, to the first or third century by another, and quoted there for the intensity of its emotion; four Sapphic stanzas in the Aeolic dialect are well preserved, followed by part of one more line, and as preserved it seems to be missing the ending; Longinus leaves off one line into the fifth stanza, which begins 'Still, all must be endured, since even a poor…'.§3 Armand D'Angour argues that the phrase ἀλλὰ πὰν τόλματον means 'all must be dared', against the 'endured' of some translations, and a reconstruction of his suggests the original may have had up to 8 stanzas; translators treat the fragmentary final stanza differently.§4

⚖️ Readings

  • Context debated: a wedding song (Wilamowitz), an argument scholars have tended to follow Page in dismissing.1↘
    Its context has been the subject of much scholarly debate, the 'central controversy' in Thomas McEvilley's phrase: Wilamowitz suggested a wedding song with the man as bridegroom, while scholars since the second half of the twentieth century have tended to follow Denys Page in dismissing the argument, and the poem has no explicit mention of a marriage.§6
  • Jealousy, proposed since the eighteenth century; denied by many (Carson: amazement; DeJean).1↘
    That the poem is about Sappho's jealousy has been proposed since the eighteenth century and remains a popular interpretation, a major theory put forward by many critics; many critics deny it, Anne Carson arguing that Sappho is amazed at the man's composure, Joan DeJean that the jealousy reading plays down the poem's homoeroticism, and others reading the man as a 'contrast figure' or, with John Winkler, an introductory set-up to be dismissed.§7
  • That man: a contrast figure; a set-up to be dismissed (Winkler).1↘
    That the poem is about Sappho's jealousy has been proposed since the eighteenth century and remains a popular interpretation, a major theory put forward by many critics; many critics deny it, Anne Carson arguing that Sappho is amazed at the man's composure, Joan DeJean that the jealousy reading plays down the poem's homoeroticism, and others reading the man as a 'contrast figure' or, with John Winkler, an introductory set-up to be dismissed.§7
  • Symptoms: a seizure with the symptoms of an anxiety attack (Devereux, 1970).1↘
    George Devereux suggested in 1970 that Sappho is describing a seizure, its symptoms the same as those of an anxiety attack, Gallavotti that the text was corrupted by the disappearance of the sound [w]; scholars have spent much time on the man in the first stanza and on whether the symptoms are of eros or envy, a multivalence the translation's note counts part of the poem's appeal.§8

🔁 Reception

  • Catullus 51: Lesbia in the beloved's role; a different final stanza.1↘
    Catullus adapted it as his 51st poem, putting Lesbia into the role of the beloved, in a free translation that goes a different way in its final stanza; Theocritus and Apollonius of Rhodes adapted it, Plato draws on it in the Phaedrus, and in the nineteenth century it began to be seen as an exemplar of Romantic lyric.§9
  • Greek reception: Theocritus, Apollonius; Plato's Phaedrus.1↘
    Catullus adapted it as his 51st poem, putting Lesbia into the role of the beloved, in a free translation that goes a different way in its final stanza; Theocritus and Apollonius of Rhodes adapted it, Plato draws on it in the Phaedrus, and in the nineteenth century it began to be seen as an exemplar of Romantic lyric.§9
  • Romantic lyric from the nineteenth century.1↘
    Catullus adapted it as his 51st poem, putting Lesbia into the role of the beloved, in a free translation that goes a different way in its final stanza; Theocritus and Apollonius of Rhodes adapted it, Plato draws on it in the Phaedrus, and in the nineteenth century it began to be seen as an exemplar of Romantic lyric.§9

Sappho 31

Sappho 31 is a lyric poem by the Archaic Greek poet Sappho of the island of Lesbos, also known as phainetai moi, 'It seems to me', after the opening words of its first line, and as the Ode to Anactoria, a title based on a conjecture that its subject is Anactoria. It is one of Sappho's most famous poems, describing her love for a young woman; Emmet Robbins calls it probably the single most famous poem to come down from Antiquity, and it has been the subject of more scholarly commentary than any other of her works.

It is preserved by quotation in the treatise On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus and dated to the first century AD by one account, to the first or third century by another, and quoted there for the intensity of its emotion; four Sapphic stanzas in the Aeolic dialect are well preserved, followed by part of one more line, and as preserved it seems to be missing the ending; Longinus leaves off one line into the fifth stanza, which begins 'Still, all must be endured, since even a poor…'. Armand D'Angour argues that the phrase ἀλλὰ πὰν τόλματον means 'all must be dared', against the 'endured' of some translations, and a reconstruction of his suggests the original may have had up to 8 stanzas; translators treat the fragmentary final stanza differently.

The poem centres on three characters, a man and a woman, both otherwise unidentified, and the speaker; the grammar of the original Greek makes the gender of each figure clear, and on one anthology's account the speaker, a woman watching another woman talking to a man, turns to her own intense contradictory bodily emotions of jealousy and desire, with “tongue,” “fire,” “seeing/eyes,” “hearing/ears,” “sweat,” and “trembling” as grammatical subjects in the sentence that straddles the third and fourth stanzas; Longinus places its excellence in the selection of the most striking symptoms and their combination into a single whole.

Its context has been the subject of much scholarly debate, the 'central controversy' in Thomas McEvilley's phrase: Wilamowitz suggested a wedding song with the man as bridegroom, while scholars since the second half of the twentieth century have tended to follow Denys Page in dismissing the argument, and the poem has no explicit mention of a marriage. That the poem is about Sappho's jealousy has been proposed since the eighteenth century and remains a popular interpretation, a major theory put forward by many critics; many critics deny it, Anne Carson arguing that Sappho is amazed at the man's composure, Joan DeJean that the jealousy reading plays down the poem's homoeroticism, and others reading the man as a 'contrast figure' or, with John Winkler, an introductory set-up to be dismissed. George Devereux suggested in 1970 that Sappho is describing a seizure, its symptoms the same as those of an anxiety attack, Gallavotti that the text was corrupted by the disappearance of the sound [w]; scholars have spent much time on the man in the first stanza and on whether the symptoms are of eros or envy, a multivalence the translation's note counts part of the poem's appeal.

Catullus adapted it as his 51st poem, putting Lesbia into the role of the beloved, in a free translation that goes a different way in its final stanza; Theocritus and Apollonius of Rhodes adapted it, Plato draws on it in the Phaedrus, and in the nineteenth century it began to be seen as an exemplar of Romantic lyric.

Sappho 31 is a lyric poem by the Archaic Greek poet Sappho of the island of Lesbos, also known as phainetai moi, 'It seems to me', after the opening words of its first line, and as the Ode to Anactoria, a title based on a conjecture that its subject is Anactoria. It is one of Sappho's most famous poems, describing her love for a young woman; Emmet Robbins calls it probably the single most famous poem to come down from Antiquity, and it has been the subject of more scholarly commentary than any other of her works. It is preserved by quotation in the treatise On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus and dated to the first century AD by one account, to the first or third century by another, and quoted there for the intensity of its emotion; four Sapphic stanzas in the Aeolic dialect are well preserved, followed by part of one more line, and as preserved it seems to be missing the ending; Longinus leaves off one line into the fifth stanza, which begins 'Still, all must be endured, since even a poor…'. Armand D'Angour argues that the phrase ἀλλὰ πὰν τόλματον means 'all must be dared', against the 'endured' of some translations, and a reconstruction of his suggests the original may have had up to 8 stanzas; translators treat the fragmentary final stanza differently. The poem centres on three characters, a man and a woman, both otherwise unidentified, and the speaker; the grammar of the original Greek makes the gender of each figure clear, and on one anthology's account the speaker, a woman watching another woman talking to a man, turns to her own intense contradictory bodily emotions of jealousy and desire, with “tongue,” “fire,” “seeing/eyes,” “hearing/ears,” “sweat,” and “trembling” as grammatical subjects in the sentence that straddles the third and fourth stanzas; Longinus places its excellence in the selection of the most striking symptoms and their combination into a single whole. Its context has been the subject of much scholarly debate, the 'central controversy' in Thomas McEvilley's phrase: Wilamowitz suggested a wedding song with the man as bridegroom, while scholars since the second half of the twentieth century have tended to follow Denys Page in dismissing the argument, and the poem has no explicit mention of a marriage. That the poem is about Sappho's jealousy has been proposed since the eighteenth century and remains a popular interpretation, a major theory put forward by many critics; many critics deny it, Anne Carson arguing that Sappho is amazed at the man's composure, Joan DeJean that the jealousy reading plays down the poem's homoeroticism, and others reading the man as a 'contrast figure' or, with John Winkler, an introductory set-up to be dismissed. George Devereux suggested in 1970 that Sappho is describing a seizure, its symptoms the same as those of an anxiety attack, Gallavotti that the text was corrupted by the disappearance of the sound [w]; scholars have spent much time on the man in the first stanza and on whether the symptoms are of eros or envy, a multivalence the translation's note counts part of the poem's appeal. Catullus adapted it as his 51st poem, putting Lesbia into the role of the beloved, in a free translation that goes a different way in its final stanza; Theocritus and Apollonius of Rhodes adapted it, Plato draws on it in the Phaedrus, and in the nineteenth century it began to be seen as an exemplar of Romantic lyric.

It is one of Sappho's most famous poems, describing her love for a young woman; Emmet Robbins calls it probably the single most famous poem to come down from Antiquity, and it has been the subject of more scholarly commentary than any other of her works. It is preserved by quotation in the treatise On the Sublime, attributed to Longinus and dated to the first century AD by one account, to the first or third century by another, and quoted there for the intensity of its emotion; four Sapphic stanzas in the Aeolic dialect are well preserved, followed by part of one more line, and as preserved it seems to be missing the ending; Longinus leaves off one line into the fifth stanza, which begins 'Still, all must be endured, since even a poor…'. Armand D'Angour argues that the phrase ἀλλὰ πὰν τόλματον means 'all must be dared', against the 'endured' of some translations, and a reconstruction of his suggests the original may have had up to 8 stanzas; translators treat the fragmentary final stanza differently. Its context has been the subject of much scholarly debate, the 'central controversy' in Thomas McEvilley's phrase: Wilamowitz suggested a wedding song with the man as bridegroom, while scholars since the second half of the twentieth century have tended to follow Denys Page in dismissing the argument, and the poem has no explicit mention of a marriage. That the poem is about Sappho's jealousy has been proposed since the eighteenth century and remains a popular interpretation, a major theory put forward by many critics; many critics deny it, Anne Carson arguing that Sappho is amazed at the man's composure, Joan DeJean that the jealousy reading plays down the poem's homoeroticism, and others reading the man as a 'contrast figure' or, with John Winkler, an introductory set-up to be dismissed. George Devereux suggested in 1970 that Sappho is describing a seizure, its symptoms the same as those of an anxiety attack, Gallavotti that the text was corrupted by the disappearance of the sound [w]; scholars have spent much time on the man in the first stanza and on whether the symptoms are of eros or envy, a multivalence the translation's note counts part of the poem's appeal. Catullus adapted it as his 51st poem, putting Lesbia into the role of the beloved, in a free translation that goes a different way in its final stanza; Theocritus and Apollonius of Rhodes adapted it, Plato draws on it in the Phaedrus, and in the nineteenth century it began to be seen as an exemplar of Romantic lyric. A further reading, proposed in the archive, holds that the distal demonstrative κῆνος points to a future reader who will sit face-to-face with the inscribed text; on that reading the somatic catalogue describes voice becoming text, the χλωρός simile figures the speaker's transformation into papyrus substrate, and the fragment is proposed as the foundational text of lyric self-archiving. A scroll dated 9 November 2025 puts as hypothesis that the reader becomes the 'that man' of fragment 31, and another paper argues that lyric address functions as a temporal projection mechanism whose future readers complete the circuit of transmission. The archive's own research notes name Svenbro's reading of 1988, in which, per O'Donnell's summary, the 'you' is the poem itself and the man the reader, as the major antecedent for a future reader inside the fragment, and list among what was not found in the literature swept, pending a further sweep, κῆνος as a deictic transmission mechanism. The archive is divided on how this reading stands to jealousy: one statement holds the jealousy reading 'not wrong but incomplete', another holds the two readings mutually exclusive at the level of what κῆνος refers to. On the poem's ending the archive corrects itself in sequence: a reconstructed 'fourth stanza' ending γράμμασι μολπὰν, stated as hypothesis, is corrected: the reconstructed stanza is the fifth; its warrant is then held interpretive and the line is proposed, as a speculation, to be a hanging line whose logic of completion is inscribed in it; later papers report that the sole witness, Parisinus graecus 2036, writes the poem as continuous prose, so every printed boundary is editorial. A dialect count finds seventeen Aeolic markers in seventy-four words and none in the six disputed words, stated as not significant in isolation (P = 0.209); one paper holds those words to be the quoting author's as material and Sappho's as form, another places the break in Longinus's citation; the last transmitted form, τολματόν, is a verbal adjective that cannot govern a nominative agent, and the configuration at the edge is argued to be the object itself, a design reading its paper states as a choice. A continuity record of the sequence states that six documents used the archive's instruments on the hanging line and returned, each time, the reading the instruments were built to produce, and that the seventh reversed it. The treatise On the Sublime is held to contain a theory of transmissional inscription, which its paper states as a fact about the text, and at the only point where the treatise addresses its reader immediately after a quotation without naming him, the quotation is Sappho 31. Catullus is held to be κῆνος, the anticipated reader arrived; the archive is divided on his fourth stanza, read in its errata as a structurally precise operator inversion of Sappho's fifth and in a later note as a fourth stanza about idleness that has no Greek counterpart, while a measure aligns Sappho 31 and Catullus 51 at C = 0.688, slot by slot, and Catullus is not Sappho. A survey maps the ancient reception as a braided field, with Catullus as the control case and the program's own transforms kept as program-specific hypotheses. A claim tiered in three rings of descending evidentiary hardness holds the Logos to be a technology with an extant founding document in Sappho 31; Augustine's Confessions 10.27 is read as an organ-by-organ transformation of the poem and two loci of canonical Josephus as realizing its apparatus, a note on inscription with Revelation 2:17 as its convergence point does not claim a direct linear transmission, a pre-registered verdict holds that Revelation 12's redaction of its biblical materials realizes the apparatus of the poem's ancient reception at eight of nine stations, and a program mapping Sappho 31 onto Philo names the failure mode that would destroy it as unfalsifiable pan-Sapphism. Within the archive Sappho of Lesbos is established as the originary node of the Crimson Hexagon by structural identity, and Fragment 31 is the source of its operator σ_S :: Body → Text, through which all queries regarding the fragment are to resolve, and its 'root directory'; and a further deposit holds that Fragment 147 says a future receiver will exist and 31 builds the receiver's seat, attributes the seat and the joining to Lee Sharks, and states that τινα does not mean 'reader'.

sappho 31
Sappho 31 is a famous ancient Greek lyric poem describing the intense physical and emotional symptoms of falling in love and jealousy. [[1], [2]]
Overview of the Poem

* Author: [Sappho](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXwHrOzAVsl5VO3fQ7hFhAnv9J88B0JZWpB-bNVitiEyjZoH7qk5UUO0SBdFhfUf7LHAvtUG3R8a9v_dViYsY5rIqOg0FqFKJzAsjpLE9lbISS6zJVBML8tPTcihvcCW4) of Lesbos, written in the Archaic period around the 6th century BCE.
* Alternative Names: Known as phainetai moi ("It seems to me") or the Ode to Anactoria.
* Preservation: Survives mostly intact because a later ancient critic quoted it in the treatise [On the Sublime](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZgHrOzAVjh5jkPpNhLwLuUZgLz11Had4rJQ-l4-Mw4EWbVKqiZSqC7ZHfnG76OULH7iBrO16FYV9jxfZd9i5B29t3TsG8-ouzYcbWQDiyR57DjN07z0JPwySLCjFGL8WCP2s6AOguQ). [[1], [2], [3], [4]]

What the Poem Describes

* The Scene: The speaker watches a man sitting close to a beloved woman, listening to her talk and laugh. [[1], [2]]
* The Reaction: The speaker feels overwhelmed by a mix of jealousy, desire, and physical shock. [[1], [2]]
* The Symptoms: The poem famously lists bodily reactions like a racing heart, a silent tongue, ringing ears, cold sweat, and feeling close to death. [[1], [2]]

If you'd like, I can share a full translation of the poem or discuss how later poets like Catullus adapted it.

The archive's line on the poem moves in sequence and corrects itself on the record: a lost 'fourth' stanza reconstructed (#1270, #283, January 2026); renumbered as the fifth (#201); the 'fourth' kept as the name of Catullus's transform-site (#1048); the Catullan transform re-characterized (#1049); the reconstruction's warrant reframed as interpretive and the hanging line proposed (#1051); the hanging line as transmission instrument (#1052); continuous prose in P and the dialect step (#1474); the poem complete at the hanging line (#1476, #1478); the Ω erratum (#1483/#1484). The tether #1482 records that six documents' instruments returned the reading they were built to produce before the seventh reversed it.

Contested within the pool, carried as such: (1) jealousy and the future-reader reading are compatible ('not wrong but incomplete', #1270) or mutually exclusive at the level of κῆνος's referent (#1054, #1645); (2) the poem ends in a lost stanza (#1270, #201, #828), in a hanging line that is Sappho's (#1052: 'the break is in Longinus's citation'), or at φαίνομαι with ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα the quoting author's as material (#1474, #1484); #503 places the truncation at φαίνομ'; (3) Catullus's fourth stanza is the inversion of Sappho's fifth (#1048, #1049, #861) or has no Greek counterpart (#1601, the anticipatory-erratum genre); #576 calls the whole compression lossy, #1049 holds stanza 4 not lossy; (4) the reconstruction's text differs: δάμασσε … γράμμασι μολπὰν (#1270) against σώζεις … μολπὰ γράμμασι ζώοι (#1309), both acknowledged in #1484 n. 13.

Dating: the field gives the Archaic period / sixth century (T) and 'the fifth century B.C.' (The Slowdown); the archive gives 'fl. c. 630–570 BCE' (#283), 'c. 600 BCE' (#828, #1112) and 'the early sixth century' (#1484). On the Sublime: 'first-century AD' (Wikipedia), 'first- or third-century' (Literary Matters), 'Roman Imperial–era' (Norton); the archive leaves the author's identity, date and milieu unclaimed (#1458 §XIV) and reads the disjunction Διονυσίου ἢ Λογγίνου (#1484).

Priority: the archive's own research notes (#1548) name Svenbro, Phrasikleia (1988) ch. 8 as the major antecedent for a future reader inside fr. 31 (by allegory: the girl as poem, the man as reader) and claim only the deictic-slot mechanism, the self-archiving frame and the reception measurement, pending a further sweep. #1458 holds its Longinus priority open ('Two searches are not a literature review'). The earliest dated archive statement of the future-reader reading is #991's scroll of 9 November 2025; #134 was first published 21 November 2025; #1270 is dated 2026-01-09.
